summary: Fever is a rise in body temperature, usually a sign that the body is fighting an infection or inflammation. It is a symptom, not a disease. Many different illnesses (including dengue, malaria, typhoid, flu, urinary and chest infections) can cause fever, so the cause must be found by a doctor.
causes: Mosquito-borne infections such as dengue and malaria
risk_factors: Diabetes, kidney disease or other chronic illness, weak immunity

tests.name: Tests chosen by the doctor according to your symptoms, duration and local disease patterns
tests.purpose: Examples a doctor may choose from: CBC, malaria test, dengue test, typhoid blood culture, urine test, chest X-ray.

preparation.fasting: Usually not required for these tests.
preparation.other: Preparation can differ between labs and between patients; follow the instructions of your doctor or lab.

tests.exceptions: There is no single test set that every person with fever needs. Do not self-select antibiotics or antimalarials.

prevention: Wash hands regularly and drink safe water
Stay up to date with recommended vaccines
lifestyle: Rest and drink plenty of safe fluids as advised by the doctor
Avoid aspirin and ibuprofen-type painkillers unless a doctor specifically advises, especially when dengue is possible
Do not start antibiotics or other medicines on your own
red_flags: Fever in a baby under 3 months
Fever lasting more than about 3 days, or rising
Difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion, stiff neck or seizures
Persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, or unable to drink
Rash, bleeding or very dark urine
Fever during pregnancy or in a person with a serious chronic illness
when_to_consult: Fever that persists for more than 2 to 3 days
Any fever with a red-flag sign
Fever in infants, pregnant women and older adults should be seen early
special_populations: Infants and children: see a paediatrician early
Pregnancy: do not wait; consult the doctor
Older adults may have a lower fever even with serious infection

faqs.q: How much temperature is considered fever?
faqs.a: Different thermometers and body sites give different readings. If you feel unwell with a raised temperature, ask a doctor how to interpret it.

faqs.q: Which test should I get for fever?
faqs.a: It depends on your symptoms and how many days you have had fever. A doctor will decide.
